en: The Sūtra on the Times of Antiquity Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Rishis. At that time, all the...
After the bhikṣus had finished their meal, they gathered in the lecture hall and discussed together:

"Suppose there is a householder whose conduct is impartial, and a bhikṣu of pure precepts who observes the true precepts comes to his house to receive alms. If he were to obtain a hundred catties of gold instead, which would be superior?"
Some bhikṣus replied to him, saying:
"Whether it be a hundred catties or a thousand catties, consider it well and calculate its benefit.
For a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, practices the true and correct path, and accepts his alms, the merit of one who keeps such a person in mind is supreme."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was present in that assembly; hearing these words of the Dharma teaching, he replied:
"How could it be merely a hundred thousand?
Even if there were treasures beyond measure exceeding this number, they would still not equal the meal-offering provided by the householder to the bhikṣus who possess the true precepts."

Why is this? I recall that in the past, when I was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, grain prices soared and the people suffered from famine; at that time, I supported myself by carrying loads of grass to sell.
In that country there was a Pratyekabuddha named Ho-li who came to travel through its lands.

Early one morning, I went out of the city intending to carry grass on my back. At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, having donned his robes and taken up his alms-bowl, entered the city to beg for food. On the way back with my load of grass, I encountered him again at the city gate as he was departing with an empty bowl.
The Pratyekabuddha Vairaṇya saw me from afar as I was approaching and thought to himself:

"I entered the city early and this man has now left it; since he is returning with grass, I suspect he has not yet eaten his morning meal. I shall follow him to his house and beg for food to satisfy my hunger."

At that time, I carried the grass back to my own house; having set the grass down on the ground, I looked back and saw the Pratyekabuddha following behind me like a shadow follows a form. I then thought to myself:

"When I went out of the city this morning, I saw this Pratyekabuddha entering the city for alms and returning with an empty bowl. I suspect he has not yet obtained food; I shall fast and offer it to him."
He immediately took the food out, knelt down on his right knee, and offered it to him, saying:
"May your person be at peace and secure; I pray that you, O Noble One, will compassionately accept this.
Then the Pratyekabuddha said:

"When grain is scarce and dear and the people suffer from hunger, one should divide it into two portions: place one portion in the bowl and eat the other oneself; this alone is in accordance with the Dharma."
The man replied to him, saying:
"Indeed, O Holy One!

As a layman living at home, I have merely prepared cooking vessels and food; there is no need for haste in preparing the meal, as it matters not whether it is early or late. I pray that you, O Practitioner, will show compassion and accept [this offering] from my household."
At that time, those pratyekabuddhas accepted all the food.
By virtue of this merit, I was born seven times in the heavens as various celestial kings, and seven times I lived among humans as the most honored among men.

Because of this single act of giving, I am seen and served by kings, elders, commoners, ministers, and officials; I am seen and provided for by the fourfold assembly of disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—with clothing, food and drink, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick. They come to me of their own accord to seek my presence, yet I have no expectations of them.

Originally born into a household as a scion of the Śākyas, various treasuries overflowed with gold, silver, and precious jewels beyond all calculation, as well as other wealth and goods that were limitless; yet he abandoned his home and renounced his worldly affairs to become a śramaṇa.
"If at that time one were to know that this person on the path will attain the way of a Pratyekabuddha, they would broaden their mind, and their merit would be immeasurable.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"I once carried grass for hire, Living as a poor laborer; ... (the rest of the verse follows)"
I made offerings to the śramaṇas, who were praised as pratyekabuddhas of the Śāri lineage.
Because of this, I was born into the Śākya clan, named Ānanda.
I became skilled in song and dance, performing on the lute, the harp, and the flute.
At that time, seeing the Teacher, the Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme nectar,
I immediately gave rise to a heart of joy and left the household life to become a śramaṇa.
Thereupon I knew my past lives and all that I had experienced in previous existences.
In that Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one experiences peace for seven lifetimes;
seven there and seven here, totaling fourteen from beginning to end,
never reaching the evil realms, whether in the heavens or the human world.
Knowing the coming and going of beings and the destinations of birth and death,
though one may find pleasure therein, it is not as sweet as the Noble Path.
By means of the fivefold concentration of mind, one becomes tranquil and single-minded.
Having washed away the manifold defilements of the fetters, one beholds purity with the eye of the Way.
For this purpose one leaves the household life; remaining at home harms one's practice.
When his vows are thus fulfilled, he brings the Buddha’s teaching to completion.
Neither do I delight in birth, nor do I delight in seeking death;
from the very beginning, I have not chosen my time, but have remained silent and fixed in my resolve.
Amidst the bamboo trees of Vaiśālī, there my life shall come to an end.
"Abiding beneath the bamboo trees, he has attained parinirvāṇa, free from outflows.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his divine ear, heard clearly how the bhikṣu Ānanda-ruci was recounting to the assembly of bhikṣus his own past lives and the rewards of the merits he had previously experienced. Emerging from his meditation chamber, he went to the lecture hall, sat before the bhikṣus, and addressed them:
"Gathered together as you are, what have you been discussing?"
The bhikṣus said:
"We have all gathered here, each discussing where offenses, blessings, good, and evil lead.
The Venerable Ānanda has himself recounted the roots of merit he cultivated in his past lives."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Since you have already recounted the events of the past, you now wish to hear the Tathāgata’s discourse on the origins of the future.
The bhikṣus said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the time; you should speak of the Dharma for the future for the sake of the bhikṣus, so that upon hearing it, they may receive and uphold it.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy."

The Buddha said: "In a future age, people shall have long lives, reaching eighty thousand years. In this Jambudvīpa, the population will be flourishing and the five grains will be abundant and cheap; people will live in settlements so close that their roosters can hear one another.

Women shall not marry until they are five hundred years old, and there will be only three afflictions: old age, illness, and the need for excretion. There will be nothing else for which they must strive or seek.
At that time, there was a king named Wei Ke, who ruled over the four continents as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja), governing by means of the True Dharma.

He naturally possessed the seven treasures: the golden wheel, the white elephant, the dark-blue horse, the bright pearl, the jade-like queen, the minister of the treasury, and the minister of the army. The king had a thousand sons, all valiant, strong, and of exceptionally handsome appearance; they subdued the armies of others and governed the four continents without the use of whips, staves, or blades, ruling through the True Dharma so that the people lived in peace and security.

The king possessed four chariots, all fashioned from the seven treasures; their wheels had a thousand spokes and were thirty-two zhang high. These chariots were exceedingly tall and majestic in their radiant splendor. Standing upon them, he raised banners and exhorted all beings to practice giving:
providing food, drink, clothing, bedding, carriages, incense, flowers, lamps, and fire to serve śramaṇas, practitioners, and the poor.
Having completed his acts of giving, he abandoned his family’s wealth, renounced his kingdom and kingship, and left the household life to study the Way as a śramaṇa.

At that time, the son of noble family, out of his aspiration for the Way, shaved off his beard and hair and donned the dharma robes; he attained the unsurpassed, pure cultivation of the brahma-faring, brought the Buddha’s teaching to its ultimate fulfillment, and spontaneously manifested the six supernormal powers in the present life. He severed the cycle of birth and death, accomplished all that was to be done, and fully understood the root of name-and-form.

At that time, the venerable Bhikṣu was present in the assembly; he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his hands joined in *añjali*, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In a future age, shall I become King Kuo?"

Did he rule over the four continents, possess the seven natural treasures, and have a thousand sons; did he govern by the True Dharma and practice extensive giving to all, and then leave the household life to study the Way and achieve unattached wisdom?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One rebuked the bhikṣu: "Foolish son!

You should have devoted this single lifetime to perfecting the Way and its virtue, yet instead you seek to wander further through birth and death, saying, 'In a future life I shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, craving the seven treasures and possessing a thousand brave sons, and only then will I enter the Path'?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"In a future age, you shall become King Kṛka, ruling over the four continents; you will extensively bestow gifts upon all, leave the household life, and attain the Way.
Thus spoke the Buddha to the bhikṣu.

"In the future, when the lifespan of humanity increases to eighty thousand years, there shall be a World-Honored One named Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—just as I am now."
Among all the devas in the heavens above and the world below—whether Brahmās, Śakras, śramaṇas, or brahmins—all without exception submit and follow to receive his teachings of the Way.

He universally expounds the Dharma-transformation for those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities, skillfully discerning their meanings and purely cultivating the holy life (brahmacarya), universally promoting the transformation of the Way just as I do now.
"This pure teaching shall spread so that throughout the heavens above and the earth below, there are none who do not receive it; the assembly of bhikṣus will be countless thousands.

At that time, the Venerable Maitreya, being present in the assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"

"In the future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, shall I, like the present Buddha, become a Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, to teach and transform those in the heavens above and the world below?"
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

You have bestowed a gentle, compliant, and vast compassion, desiring to save countless and infinite multitudes. You have given rise to this intention, wishing to act as a guide for all beings in the future, just as I am now.”

In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, to be known as Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha holding a fan.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Bring the robe woven with golden threads; I shall bestow it upon the bhikṣu Maitreya."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately went to fetch it and presented it to the World-Honored One.
Having taken it, the World-Honored One gave it to Maitreya and said to him:
"Take this Dharma robe and bestow it upon the assembly of monks."
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, brings great benefit to many people in the world and rescues them through his supreme virtue.
Maitreya then offered it to the community of monks.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"I shall go before those bhikṣus as they discourse upon the future world and now seek to disrupt their Dharma teachings.
Thereupon, Māra immediately went before the World-Honored One and spoke in verse:
"I imagine that the people of that time Will have supple bodies and beautiful hair."
His body is adorned with necklaces of various jewels, and his head is decorated with pearl-flower ornaments.
Thereupon the World-Honored One said:
“Now Māra Pāpīyas has come here on purpose, wishing to disturb the Way and its teachings.”
The Buddha then replied to Māra with a verse, saying:
"At that time, the people of the world Were free from attachment and their doubts severed;
They cast off the net of birth and death, Having accomplished their task, they were without outflows."
"In the teaching of Maitreya Buddha, I shall purely cultivate the holy life.
Thereupon, the celestial Māra again addressed the World-Honored One in verse, saying:
"I imagine that the people of that time / Will have bodies and garments of brilliant patterns."
"Anointed with sandalwood paste, adorning his body and head,
he dwells in the city of Kukkutavati, the seat of King Kesi.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied to Māra in verse:
"At that time, people will be sincere; Free from self and free from what is received, They will not use rare or exotic things, And their minds will have no greed or attachment.
Living in the world of Maitreya, They will purely cultivate the holy life."
The Mara spoke again to the Buddha in verse:
"I imagine that the people of that time will crave jewels and fine food,
becoming skilled in song and dance, delighting only in playing the lute and the zither."
He is at the tip of the rooster’s head, where King Ke resides.
Then the Buddha replied to Māra with a verse:
“That person has attained the perfections; having destroyed the net, he is unrestrained.”
"Practicing meditative concentration with equanimity, he rejoices without any attachment.
Māra Pāpīyas, you should know this: you have been cast down to the ground.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
“The Tathāgata is holy; he already knows the arising and ceasing of my dwelling place.
Distressed and unhappy, he departed in shame.
When the Buddha spoke these words, there was no one who did not rejoice.
The Sūtra on the Times of Ancient Worlds Spoken by the Buddha
